claims.text: The baseline alloy HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
The baseline alloy HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The baseline alloy HfZrTiTa0.53 has 13.5% tensile strain to failure.
Substituting approximately 2 at% Nb for part of the base alloy produces HfZrTiNbTa0.53.
Nb addition will refine grain boundaries and modify the phase distribution through solid-solution effects.
Nb will reduce localized stress concentrations and promote more uniform plasticity.
Nb addition will enhance grain-boundary stability.
Nb addition may facilitate a more ductile phase or reduce embrittling segregation.
The proposed microstructural changes will improve tensile uniform elongation.
The Nb-modified alloy will increase tensile uniform elongation by approximately 50%, from 13.5% toward 20%.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain yield and compressive strengths within 10% of the baseline values.
The Nb-modified alloy will show no significant decrease in impact-triggered energy release.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has demonstrated high impact-triggered energy release through tungsten-alloy penetration comparisons.
The predicted tensile and compressive improvements apply at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
The predicted preservation of energetic behavior applies under impact conditions analogous to thin-steel-target penetration.
Alloying strategies in refractory multicomponent alloys provide prior support for the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The text specifies approximately 2 at% Nb, but the formula HfZrTiNbTa0.53 assigns Nb a coefficient of 1 and therefore about 22.1 at% after normalization. The formula also adds a full Nb component rather than clearly substituting 2 at% for specified base elements.
The hypothesis describes the modification as adding Nb, whereas the intervention describes it as substitution; these imply different normalization and retention of the original elements.

The same 13.5% value is variously labeled tensile strain to failure and tensile uniform elongation. These are distinct mechanical metrics and cannot be treated as interchangeable without evidence that necking did not separate them.
